stem: A data science team is developing an automated pipeline that integrates Amazon SageMaker AI and Amazon Comprehend to analyze large volumes of customer feedback data. The team first uses a PySpark script running on Amazon EMR to perform text preprocessing, tokenization, and feature engineering on millions of feedback records stored in Amazon S3. The preprocessed data is then passed to Comprehend for sentiment and entity extraction, and subsequently used to train multiple sentiment classification models in SageMaker AI. The AI developer must determine how varying the PySpark feature transformation parameters and sample sizes affects overall model accuracy and inference performance. Which solution will meet this requirement most effectively?

options.text: Use SageMaker Debugger hook to capture feature engineering metrics and execution logs during PySpark script execution within a SageMaker training job.
options.rationale: because SageMaker Debugger is primarily designed to monitor and profile training jobs, not preprocessing scripts. It captures internal model states like tensors and gradients, but it doesn’t support logging PySpark parameters or tracking preprocessing variations in a structured way.

options.text: Use SageMaker Experiments tracker to log PySpark parameters and model metrics while executing the script as a SageMaker processing job.
Use SageMaker Model Monitor to detect differences in PySpark data transformation parameters before each training iteration.
options.rationale: because Model Monitor is typically used for post-deployment monitoring of data drift and model quality in production endpoints. It does not track preprocessing parameters or support experimentation during training or processing jobs.

options.text: Use SageMaker Autopilot to automatically choose the best PySpark preprocessing configuration and feature-engineering parameters for model optimization.
options.rationale: because Autopilot automates preprocessing and model selection using its own internal logic. It does not support custom PySpark scripts or manual control over feature engineering parameters, which are essential for the team’s experimentation goals.

correct_text: Use SageMaker Experiments tracker to log PySpark parameters and model metrics while executing the script as a SageMaker processing job.

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A company uses a customer relationship management (CRM) platform to manage its sales pipeline, support tickets, and account health. The company is developing a generative AI assistant that can compose personalized email outreach, summarize recent customer interactions, and provide actionable recommendations for account management. Sales and support data are stored in Amazon S3 and other internal file storage. The engineering team requires the data pipelines to run continuously, ensuring the assistant always has access to fresh data for generation and training, while minimizing manual ETL tasks. To enhance the solution, the team plans to leverage Amazon Comprehend to extract sentiment, customer issues, and entity metadata from unstructured support logs. Amazon SageMaker AI is used to train predictive models for customer engagement scoring based on historical interactions and CRM activity. The solution must automatically ingest and process CRM data, combine insights from Comprehend and SageMaker AI, and feed the results into a foundation model pipeline for retraining or inference without requiring constant manual intervention. Which approach offers the most scalable and reliable method for automating the CRM data processing pipeline?

options.text: Use Amazon EventBridge to trigger AWS Lambda functions whenever new CRM data is added to S3. Set up a Lambda function to preprocess the data, call Comprehend for sentiment analysis, and push the output to SageMaker AI for model retraining.
options.rationale: . Using Lambda to orchestrate preprocessing, Comprehend analysis, and SageMaker retraining introduces operational complexity and is simply not ideal for large volumes of CRM data. Lambda functions have execution time limits and concurrency constraints, making this method only partially automated and less reliable for continuous retraining pipelines.

options.text: Export CRM data to S3 every week, run a SageMaker Notebook to transform the data, call Comprehend, and feed the output into the foundation model retraining.
options.rationale: . This workflow is just a periodic, manual process that updates models on a weekly schedule. It does not provide the continuous data availability that a production-ready generative AI assistant requires. As a result, insights and retrained models can become outdated, making this approach typically inefficient for real-time decision-making and personalized recommendations.

options.text: Connect to CRM data using SageMaker Data Wrangler, perform transformations, and analyze text with Comprehend. Run SageMaker AI training jobs separately and manually trigger foundation model retraining in Amazon Bedrock.
options.rationale: . This method offers some automation for data transformation but still depends on manual execution for model training and foundation model retraining. It is simply not fully integrated into an end-to-end automated workflow, which increases operational burden. This approach is primarily suitable for experimental or development environments rather than a scalable, production-grade AI solution.

options.text: Configure Amazon Bedrock Data Automation to continuously ingest CRM data from S3. Apply preprocessing, including sentiment and entity extraction with Comprehend, and automatically load the enriched data into retraining pipelines for SageMaker AI and foundation models.

correct_text: Configure Amazon Bedrock Data Automation to continuously ingest CRM data from S3. Apply preprocessing, including sentiment and entity extraction with Comprehend, and automatically load the enriched data into retraining pipelines for SageMaker AI and foundation models.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A large financial services company is developing an internal generative AI application to assist customer support agents in drafting responses to complex client inquiries. Historical support-ticket transcripts and sensitive client data are stored in Amazon S3. Data engineers preprocess the transcripts in Amazon SageMaker Studio, performing tokenization, anonymization, and vector embedding. The company fine-tunes a foundation model obtained via SageMaker JumpStart on this proprietary dataset and deploys it as a real-time endpoint. Agents interact with the model through an internal chat UI, which integrates a company knowledge base via a vector search index in Amazon OpenSearch Service. To comply with internal security policies and industry regulations, the company must accurately map the Generative AI Security Scoping Matrix and implement all necessary security controls, including data handling, encryption, and model governance. Which best describes the appropriate scope and key security responsibility for this generative AI workload?

options.text: The workload falls under Scope 3: Pre-trained models. The company is responsible for reviewing the foundation model’s license and terms of service to confirm that proprietary client data is not inadvertently used for further training by the vendor.
options.rationale: . While Scope 3 workloads typically involve minimal control over the model and only require review of licensing and terms of service, in this scenario, the company is actively fine-tuning the foundation model on proprietary data. Therefore, the organization’s responsibilities extend beyond ensuring vendor compliance to include securing the training dataset, managing fine-tuned model versions, and enforcing governance, which is characteristic of Scope 4.

options.text: The workload falls under Scope 4: Fine-tuned models. The company must ensure that all proprietary training data is classified, encrypted at rest and in transit, access is strictly controlled, and an audit trail of model versions, data lineage, and fine-tuning processes is maintained.

The workload falls under Scope 2: Enterprise applications. The company’s main responsibility is to enforce contractual terms, service-level agreements, and vendor data-use restrictions because the generative AI model is accessed only via a third-party managed service.
options.rationale: . Scope 2 generally applies when organizations rely on managed SaaS or enterprise AI products and their responsibilities are mostly contractual, focusing on SLAs and vendor data-use restrictions. In this case, the company is directly handling and fine-tuning the model, which requires more comprehensive security and governance measures than simply enforcing vendor agreements.

options.text: The workload falls under Scope 5: Self-trained models. The company must assume full ownership of the model infrastructure, including GPU clusters, training pipelines, security configurations, and governance processes for model release and versioning.
options.rationale: . Scope 5 applies when an organization builds a generative AI model entirely on internal infrastructure, assuming full responsibility for GPU clusters, training pipelines, and model governance from end to end. In this scenario, the company is fine-tuning an existing foundation model using SageMaker JumpStart, thereby avoiding the need to manage all underlying infrastructure or create a model entirely from scratch. The security responsibilities are significant, but they align with Scope 4 rather than Scope 5.

correct_text: The workload falls under Scope 4: Fine-tuned models. The company must ensure that all proprietary training data is classified, encrypted at rest and in transit, access is strictly controlled, and an audit trail of model versions, data lineage, and fine-tuning processes is maintained.

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A financial analytics firm uses Amazon SageMaker AI and Amazon Comprehend to detect potential fraud patterns across millions of real-time financial transactions. Comprehend extracts critical text features such as transaction context, merchant type, and sentiment from unstructured financial notes, while SageMaker AI consumes this enriched dataset to train and deploy a fraud detection model that classifies transactions as legitimate or suspicious. A newly optimized model version has recently been retrained in SageMaker AI using improved training features and hyperparameters. The data science team must evaluate the new model’s prediction accuracy and latency in production without impacting the throughput of the currently deployed model. Additionally, the deployment process must introduce minimal operational overhead and must not require any changes to the way the inference endpoint is invoked by clients. Which of the following options will satisfy the given requirements?

options.text: Register the new model version in SageMaker Model Registry and configure an event trigger in AWS Lambda to automatically swap the endpoint to the new model after initial validation.
options.rationale: because it primarily replaces the existing model entirely, preventing side-by-side evaluation. This approach risks production stability and introduces unnecessary complexity with Lambda automation and registry workflows.

options.text: Deploy both models in separate SageMaker endpoints and use Amazon CloudWatch metrics to compare their results in post-processing.
options.rationale: because it typically requires managing multiple endpoints and manually routing traffic, which increases operational overhead. It also violates the requirement that clients should not have to change how they invoke the inference endpoint.

options.text: Configure an Amazon API Gateway endpoint that splits traffic between the current and the new SageMaker endpoints for A/B testing.
options.rationale: because it introduces additional infrastructure and requires clients to invoke a new API Gateway endpoint instead of the existing SageMaker endpoint. This contradicts the requirement of maintaining the same client invocation method.

options.text: Modify the existing SageMaker AI endpoint configuration by adding the new model as a ProductionVariant through the ProductionVariant API, and set a small InitialVariantWeight compared to the existing model’s ProductionVariant VariantWeight to control the percentage of traffic routed to it.

correct_text: Modify the existing SageMaker AI endpoint configuration by adding the new model as a ProductionVariant through the ProductionVariant API, and set a small InitialVariantWeight compared to the existing model’s ProductionVariant VariantWeight to control the percentage of traffic routed to it.

category: AIP – Testing, Validation, and Troubleshooting
stem: A data analytics company is developing a personalized news recommendation platform that delivers tailored article suggestions to readers. The AI development team uses Amazon Comprehend to perform sentiment analysis and entity recognition on articles and reader feedback data. The extracted insights are then stored in Amazon S3 and used by an Amazon Personalize solution to generate ranked recommendations for each user session. The company has trained multiple recommendation models to improve model accuracy and wants to evaluate the effectiveness through A/B testing in a beta production environment. The system must route live inference traffic between multiple model variants, monitor real-time engagement metrics, and seamlessly direct 100% of traffic to the best-performing model. Which solution will meet these requirements in the most operationally efficient way?

options.text: Use Amazon SageMaker AI multi-variant endpoints to deploy all model versions behind a single endpoint. Configure traffic weights for A/B testing and update routing to send all inference requests to the best-performing model once identified.
Deploy the models on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to perform A/B testing, then manually adjust the ALB weights when a model shows higher engagement.
options.rationale: because it requires significant manual setup and ongoing management. You would need to handle model deployment, scaling, monitoring, and traffic routing yourself, which increases operational complexity and reduces efficiency compared to managed services like SageMaker.

options.text: Create a separate Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint for each model and configure Amazon API Gateway to distribute traffic for A/B testing based on weighted routing rules.
options.rationale: because while technically feasible, it introduces unnecessary complexity. Managing multiple endpoints and configuring API Gateway for traffic splitting and monitoring typically adds operational overhead. It also lacks the native integration and streamlined monitoring that SageMaker multi-variant endpoints provide.

options.text: Use AWS CodeDeploy with blue/green deployment strategies and an Application Load Balancer (ALB) to alternate traffic between model versions during A/B testing. Gradually route 100% of traffic to the model with the highest engagement metrics.
options.rationale: because CodeDeploy’s blue/green strategy is primarily designed for application deployments, not real-time ML inference. It doesn’t support fine-grained traffic splitting or real-time inference metric tracking, making it unsuitable for dynamic A/B testing of ML models.

correct_text: Use Amazon SageMaker AI multi-variant endpoints to deploy all model versions behind a single endpoint. Configure traffic weights for A/B testing and update routing to send all inference requests to the best-performing model once identified.

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A media technology company is building a real-time generative AI (GenAI) application that enhances live video streams with contextual overlays. The application uses a foundation model (FM) in Amazon Bedrock to generate captions and insights from incoming video frames. The solution must achieve ultra-low latency of under 20 milliseconds for mobile users, process inference requests as close to end users as possible, provide shared file storage for intermediate artifacts, and optimize prompt handling to reduce token usage during high-traffic bursts. Which solution best meets these requirements?

options.text: Deploy the application in AWS Wavelength Zones using Amazon EC2 integrated with Bedrock for inference. Use Amazon EFS for shared file storage of intermediate artifacts and implement context pruning to dynamically reduce prompt size during high-traffic bursts.

Deploy the application in a single AWS Region using Amazon EC2 instances and integrate with Bedrock. Store intermediate artifacts in Amazon S3 and increase model response size limits to improve output quality.
Use AWS Lambda with Bedrock in a centralized Region. Store session data in Redis OSS on Amazon ElastiCache and apply fixed-size chunking to all prompts to standardize processing.
options.rationale: because centralized Lambda execution does not meet ultra-low latency requirements. Fixed-size chunking primarily lacks adaptability and can result in inefficient token usage compared to dynamic techniques such as context pruning.

options.text: Deploy the application across multiple Availability Zones within a Region using Amazon EC2. Use Amazon EBS for shared storage across instances and rely on token burst patterns to manage peak request volumes.
options.rationale: because Availability Zones are still confined within a Region and do not provide edge-level latency. Amazon EBS does not support shared access across multiple instances, and token burst patterns simply describe traffic behavior rather than optimizing token usage.

correct_text: Deploy the application in AWS Wavelength Zones using Amazon EC2 integrated with Bedrock for inference. Use Amazon EFS for shared file storage of intermediate artifacts and implement context pruning to dynamically reduce prompt size during high-traffic bursts.

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A global insurance provider processes tens of thousands of scanned policy agreements, claim submissions, and regulatory filings every day. To extract textual content from a variety of unstructured documents, the company utilizes Amazon Textract. After the data is extracted, Amazon Comprehend analyzes it to identify and classify key entities such as policy identifiers and coverage terms, while Comprehend Medical focuses on identifying medical conditions and related terminology. However, challenges arise due to inconsistent formatting, variations in terminology, abbreviations, and inaccuracies in optical character recognition (OCR), which can impede accurate entity recognition and large-scale data extraction. Certain documents fail automated validation workflows, necessitating intervention by a team of human analysts. This manual review process creates operational bottlenecks, prolongs turnaround times, and increases processing costs. The organization seeks to streamline document processing. The new workflow should reduce reliance on manual review while maintaining high precision and recall in extracted data, ensuring that downstream systems can reliably consume the information for decision-making and compliance purposes. What is the most effective way to improve automated insurance application processing?

options.text: Deploy an Amazon Bedrock’s Claude model to re-analyze low-confidence extracted insurance application text to refine validation predictions, then route the outputs for manual review.
options.rationale: because Amazon Bedrock is primarily designed for accessing and deploying foundation models for text generation, summarization, and conversational AI. It does not provide built-in capabilities for human-in-the-loop validation or confidence-based review workflows. Bedrock does not integrate directly with Amazon Textract to route low-confidence predictions for verification, making it unsuitable for document validation scenarios.

options.text: Use Textract to flag words with low confidence and send them to Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth for manual inspection before validation.
options.rationale: because SageMaker Ground Truth is only intended for building and managing labeled datasets for training or retraining machine learning models. It is not meant for real-time document validation or human review of production workloads. Ground Truth lacks native integration with Textract for automated verification workflows, so it cannot effectively address the need for continuous document accuracy checks.

options.text: Set up Textract to forward low-confidence predictions to Amazon Augmented AI (Amazon A2I) for verification prior to executing validation workflows.
Further automate insurance application validation by sending extracted text to an Amazon Titan foundation model to predict errors without human review.
options.rationale: because Titan models are typically used for generative AI tasks such as content creation or text embedding, not for deterministic validation of OCR accuracy. Also, using a foundation model without human verification would simply increase the likelihood of data errors or misinterpretations, as these models are not designed to replace confidence scoring or human review in compliance-driven document processing.

correct_text: Set up Textract to forward low-confidence predictions to Amazon Augmented AI (Amazon A2I) for verification prior to executing validation workflows.

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A company manages a large-scale analytics platform that stores high-volume transaction data in a PostgreSQL database. The dataset includes hundreds of millions of records with customer details, purchase amounts, product categories, and regions. The analytics team wants to use Amazon SageMaker AI to predict which customers are likely to churn in the next 90 days and improve retention strategies. The company needs a solution that automates data extraction and preparation from the PostgreSQL database for scheduled cleaning, normalization, and handling of missing values. After refining the data, the team considers using SageMaker Feature Store to store and manage customer features for consistent inputs in machine learning workflows. Analysts should then be able to build and deploy a no-code churn-prediction model and easily generate predictions on new customer data without support from data scientists. Some architects also evaluated Amazon DocumentDB for the future modernization of application workloads. Which is the best option to achieve this requirement?

options.text: Use AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) to replicate data from the PostgreSQL database into Amazon S3 continuously. Use AWS Glue DataBrew to clean and normalize the replicated dataset before importing it into SageMaker Canvas to build and deploy the churn-prediction model.
options.rationale: . While DMS is a powerful real-time data migration and synchronization service, it is primarily intended for scenarios requiring ongoing replication or minimal downtime migrations. In this case, the data extraction is periodic rather than continuous, so DMS would simply add unnecessary complexity and cost to the workflow. The scenario focuses on scheduled data preparation and no-code model building, not on maintaining a live replication pipeline.

options.text: Use AWS Glue DataBrew to extract and clean the dataset from PostgreSQL. Apply AWS Glue Data Quality to define and validate data quality rules, then attempt to build the churn-prediction model directly within DataBrew.
options.rationale: . AWS Glue DataBrew is primarily designed for visual data preparation, while AWS Glue Data Quality focuses on defining and validating data quality rules. Neither service supports training, deploying, or generating predictions from machine learning models. The requirement clearly states that analysts must build and deploy a no-code churn-prediction model, which DataBrew and Data Quality cannot provide. Therefore, this option only addresses data preparation and validation but fails to deliver the no-code ML modeling and prediction capabilities required in the scenario.

options.text: Use AWS Glue DataBrew to extract the data from PostgreSQL, clean and normalize the dataset, and write the prepared data back into Amazon S3. Import the cleaned dataset into SageMaker Canvas to build a no-code churn-prediction model and generate predictions for business analysts.

Use AWS Glue DataBrew to prepare and clean the data from the PostgreSQL database. Use SageMaker Studio to build, train, and deploy a custom churn-prediction model using a notebook-based workflow for data scientists.
options.rationale: . SageMaker Studio is typically designed for data scientists who build models using code and notebook-based workflows. The requirement clearly specifies a no-code solution that allows business analysts to create and generate churn predictions independently. Since Studio requires technical expertise and coding, it does not meet the no-code requirement of the scenario.

correct_text: Use AWS Glue DataBrew to extract the data from PostgreSQL, clean and normalize the dataset, and write the prepared data back into Amazon S3. Import the cleaned dataset into SageMaker Canvas to build a no-code churn-prediction model and generate predictions for business analysts.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A streaming media company is using Amazon Bedrock to power a customer support chatbot. The chatbot must handle over 60,000 subscriber inquiries daily, with spikes reaching 180,000 inquiries per day during major content releases. Analysis of historical logs shows that 35% of inquiries share nearly identical context, such as billing questions or password reset requests. A GenAI engineer must design a solution that ensures low latency and consistent performance during these traffic spikes. The team briefly considered Bedrock Agents to orchestrate multi-step inquiry handling but determined it added unnecessary complexity for this particular latency and cost problem. Which of the following solutions will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: Turn on latency-optimized inference for the chatbot's requests by switching the performance configuration's latency setting to optimized when invoking Amazon Bedrock. Pair this with prompt caching so previously seen conversation context does not need to be reprocessed for similar inquiries.

Acquire Provisioned Throughput with several model units (MUs) large enough to absorb the highest expected traffic volume. Layer in Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS) as a separate caching tier to serve answers to commonly repeated questions.
options.rationale: . Provisioned Throughput requires committing to and paying for a fixed level of model capacity, which is a fit for steady, predictable workloads, not workloads that spike from 60,000 to 180,000 inquiries a day. Sizing model units for peak load means paying for idle capacity during normal periods, which is not cost-effective. Adding a self-managed Amazon ElastiCache layer also introduces infrastructure the team must provision, secure, and maintain, unlike Bedrock’s built-in prompt caching.

options.text: Configure Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing to automatically direct inquiries to the most cost-effective foundation model based on complexity. Combine this with cross-Region inference to distribute traffic across Regions.
options.rationale: . Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing is simply designed to route each request to the FM best suited for it based on complexity, optimizing cost and quality trade-offs, not specifically to reduce latency during traffic spikes. While cross-Region inference helps distribute load, this option does not directly address the repetitive-context inquiries the way prompt caching does, making it a less targeted solution for this specific cost and latency requirement.

options.text: Use Bedrock Model Distillation to create a smaller, distilled model from a larger teacher model, and route all customer inquiries through the distilled model to reduce response time.
options.rationale: . Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation is intended primarily to produce a smaller, cheaper, faster model trained on outputs from a larger teacher model, which requires a training and evaluation process before deployment. It is not designed as an immediate, on-demand latency control for unpredictable daily traffic spikes, and it does not specifically exploit the repeated-context nature of 35-40% of the inquiries the way prompt caching does. Building and validating a distilled model also adds development time and ongoing maintenance compared to enabling built-in latency-optimized inference and prompt caching.

correct_text: Turn on latency-optimized inference for the chatbot's requests by switching the performance configuration's latency setting to optimized when invoking Amazon Bedrock. Pair this with prompt caching so previously seen conversation context does not need to be reprocessed for similar inquiries.

category: AIP – Testing, Validation, and Troubleshooting
stem: A financial services company has deployed a binary classification model to an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint to predict loan default risk. After operating in production for several months, the data science team suspects the model’s accuracy has degraded due to changes in applicant demographics and economic conditions. The team needs a solution that automatically detects when the statistical distribution of incoming inference data deviates from the training data baseline. The solution must also schedule periodic monitoring jobs without manual intervention and publish drift-violation metrics to Amazon CloudWatch for automated alerting. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST amount of operational overhead?

options.text: Enable data capture on the SageMaker real-time endpoint and use SageMaker Model Monitor to create a statistical baseline from the training dataset. Configure a monitoring schedule to automatically compare incoming inference data against the baseline constraints and publish drift violation metrics to CloudWatch.

Enable SageMaker Clarify on the real-time endpoint to run recurring bias and distribution reports on captured inference data. Configure Clarify to compare live inference payloads against the training data distribution and route deviation results to CloudWatch as custom metrics for threshold alerting.
options.rationale: because Amazon SageMaker Clarify is designed specifically for detecting bias drift and explaining feature attributions, it is not a data quality monitoring service. Clarify simply cannot independently create a statistical data quality baseline, schedule periodic data quality monitoring jobs, or publish raw distribution drift metrics to CloudWatch without Model Monitor orchestrating those steps.

options.text: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke an AWS Lambda function on a periodic schedule. Program the function to retrieve captured inference data from Amazon S3, compute distribution statistics against the training dataset baseline, and publish drift measurements as custom metrics to CloudWatch for alerting.
options.rationale: . Although this architecture can technically fulfill the requirements, it requires significant custom engineering. This includes writing and maintaining Lambda code to compute statistical drift, manage S3 data retrieval, and format CloudWatch metrics. These tasks introduce unnecessary operational overhead compared to using the purpose-built, fully managed capabilities of Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.

options.text: Build a scheduled SageMaker Pipeline with a data quality processing step that ingests captured endpoint inference data from Amazon S3, calculates statistical deviations from the training baseline, and emits the resulting drift metrics to CloudWatch at the completion of each pipeline run.
options.rationale: because Amazon SageMaker Pipelines is a CI/CD orchestration service built for automating ML training, evaluation, and deployment workflows – not for production model monitoring. It simply has no built-in baseline constraints, monitoring schedules, or drift violation reporting, meaning the team would need to author, test, and maintain all of that logic as custom code, which directly contradicts the requirement for the least operational overhead.

correct_text: Enable data capture on the SageMaker real-time endpoint and use SageMaker Model Monitor to create a statistical baseline from the training dataset. Configure a monitoring schedule to automatically compare incoming inference data against the baseline constraints and publish drift violation metrics to CloudWatch.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A healthcare organization is building an enterprise search tool using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The underlying corporate data resides in an Amazon S3 data lake, which is cataloged using AWS Glue. The organization must enforce strict access controls to ensure that different departments can only query documents that correspond to specific departmental data. The security team wants to implement fine-grained access control at the database, table, and column level using a scalable, attribute-based approach rather than managing complex AWS IAM policies for every individual user and resource combination. Which solution will securely meet these requirements with the least operational overhead?

options.text: Implement AWS Lake Formation and assign an LF-Tag to the databases, tables, and columns representing the departmental data. Grant IAM principals access to the data lake resources based on the matching LF-Tag expressions.

Use Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data within the S3 buckets. Trigger an AWS Lambda function to move the sensitive documents into separate, department-specific S3 buckets with strict bucket policies.
options.rationale: because Amazon Macie is a data security service that discovers sensitive data; it is not an access control management system for data catalogs and does not support column-level filtering.

options.text: Utilize AWS CloudFormation Guard to enforce policy-as-code rules on the Glue Data Catalog. Ensure that the queries generated by Bedrock are validated against the authorized schema before execution.
options.rationale: because CloudFormation Guard is just an open-source evaluation tool for validating infrastructure-as-code templates against compliance rules, not a runtime query interception or data access control tool.

options.text: Configure IAM identity-based policies with resource tags. Attach these policies to the roles assumed by the Bedrock Knowledge Bases to restrict access to specific S3 buckets based on department tags.
options.rationale: because AWS IAM policies and standard resource tags primarily control access at the bucket or object level, failing to provide the column-level and table-level fine-grained access required by the security team.

correct_text: Implement AWS Lake Formation and assign an LF-Tag to the databases, tables, and columns representing the departmental data. Grant IAM principals access to the data lake resources based on the matching LF-Tag expressions.

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A financial services organization is developing a generative AI chatbot using Amazon Bedrock to answer confidential customer questions. The solution must implement layered protection mechanisms to prevent advanced prompt injection attacks targeting the model. Security engineers also require detailed audit records whenever safety rules intervene, such as when model input or output is blocked or modified. In addition, the architecture must support multi-Region resilience so the AI assistant continues functioning if a Region becomes unavailable. Which architecture satisfies these requirements?

options.text: Enable Bedrock guardrails with strict content filters and attach AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) to the API endpoint to inspect incoming requests. Record activity using AWS CloudTrail API event logs.
options.rationale: because these services operate primarily at the network/API layer rather than the generative model safety layer. WAF can filter HTTP requests and block malicious patterns, but prompt injection occurs inside the model prompt context, which WAF cannot reliably analyze. Additionally, CloudTrail records API activity, not guardrail intervention events, meaning detailed AI safety actions would not be captured.

options.text: Implement Amazon Comprehend custom classifiers to detect prompt injection attacks before requests reach the model. Use Amazon API Gateway request validation and export logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
options.rationale: because this design just introduces custom NLP classifiers to detect prompt injection attempts. Prompt injection techniques often exploit model-specific prompt behavior, which traditional NLP classifiers may fail to detect reliably. Although CloudWatch Logs could capture events, this option still lacks Bedrock-native guardrail enforcement and cross-Region guardrail capabilities.

options.text: Configure Bedrock guardrails with strict word filters and enable multi-Region deployment of the application with log auditing stored in AWS CloudTrail.
options.rationale: because it relies mainly on word filters and application multi-Region deployment. Simple keyword or word filters are insufficient to detect sophisticated prompt injection patterns, which often rely on contextual manipulation rather than specific keywords. Furthermore, CloudTrail logs API-level operations, not detailed guardrail intervention events such as blocked prompts or filtered responses.

options.text: Configure Bedrock guardrails with content filters set to a high threshold to mitigate prompt injection attacks. Apply a guardrail profile to enable cross-Region guardrail inference. Send detailed guardrail intervention logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs and create custom metrics for monitoring.

correct_text: Configure Bedrock guardrails with content filters set to a high threshold to mitigate prompt injection attacks. Apply a guardrail profile to enable cross-Region guardrail inference. Send detailed guardrail intervention logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs and create custom metrics for monitoring.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A company has developed a machine learning-based recommendation system designed to personalize content for users. The model has been trained using Amazon SageMaker AI built-in algorithms and a custom dataset, with real-time inference being performed within SageMaker AI. As part of the system, the company also intends to leverage Amazon Comprehend for natural language processing to analyze customer reviews and sentiment, which will further enhance the recommendation engine. To meet strict security and compliance requirements, the company must ensure that both the training and inference environments, as well as all associated services, are deployed within a secure Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). Furthermore, the solution must completely block all access to the internet or any external resources to protect sensitive user data and ensure compliance with regulatory standards. Which of the following will satisfy the given requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Set up SageMaker AI within a VPC only mode and establish a VPC peering connection to enable Comprehend access in a different VPC.
options.rationale: because VPC peering introduces additional complexity in routing, security group configuration, and maintenance. It typically requires careful setup to ensure no unintended internet access is allowed, which increases development effort and risk.

options.text: Deploy SageMaker AI in VPC only mode and configure an internet gateway with restrictive security group rules to block external access.
options.rationale: because the presence of an internet gateway contradicts the requirement to completely block internet access. Security group rules alone cannot guarantee full isolation, and the existence of an internet gateway introduces the possibility of misconfiguration or accidental exposure, which would fail compliance audits.

options.text: Activate SageMaker AI network isolation mode to block all external access and establish a VPC endpoint for Comprehend within the same VPC.
Use VPC only mode for SageMaker AI, configure a network access control list (NACL) to block internet access, and allow traffic to Comprehend.
options.rationale: because NACLs (Network Access Control Lists) are not sufficient to fully block all external access and provide the same level of security as SageMaker’s network isolation mode. While NACLs can primarily restrict internet access, they do not provide complete isolation from external resources, as traffic could still flow via routes other than the NACLs. Moreover, this option does not use VPC endpoints to securely connect to Amazon Comprehend, leaving room for potential security risks.

correct_text: Activate SageMaker AI network isolation mode to block all external access and establish a VPC endpoint for Comprehend within the same VPC.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A large retail company is looking to leverage Amazon SageMaker AI notebooks and Amazon Comprehend to process and analyze customer feedback data. The company uses Amazon S3 buckets to store large datasets of customer reviews, and the data needs to be accessed securely for machine learning analysis. Given the sensitivity of the data, the company mandates that all resources must remain within a secure Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC). Additionally, all communication must occur over the AWS network. Which solution will satisfy the given requirements?

options.text: Deploy the SageMaker AI notebook in a private subnet with a route to an internet gateway and ensure that all data requests to S3 are routed through an external proxy.
options.rationale: because routing through an internet gateway and external proxy exposes traffic to the public internet, violating the requirement that all communication must occur over a private AWS network.

options.text: Deploy the SageMaker AI notebook in a private subnet within a VPC and use a VPC Peering connection with another VPC where S3 is accessible.
options.rationale: because VPC peering does not typically provide private access to AWS services like S3. Accessing S3 through a peered VPC still requires public endpoints unless VPC endpoints are configured, which this option does not guarantee.

options.text: Deploy the SageMaker AI notebook in a private subnet within a VPC and ensure that the VPC has private endpoints for both SageMaker AI and S3.
Deploy the SageMaker AI notebook in a private subnet, use a NAT gateway to provide outbound internet access for S3, and restrict access to only specific S3 buckets.
options.rationale: because using a NAT gateway primarily involves public internet routing, which contradicts the mandate for a private AWS network. Even with bucket restrictions, the traffic path does not meet the security requirements.

correct_text: Deploy the SageMaker AI notebook in a private subnet within a VPC and ensure that the VPC has private endpoints for both SageMaker AI and S3.

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A national utility company manages hourly power consumption data for 150 types of smart meters deployed across multiple regions. Over the past 30 years, the company has collected a large volume of historical usage data enriched with weather metrics, regional energy prices, and maintenance logs. The data science team currently uses Amazon SageMaker AI Data Wrangler to perform feature engineering and data preprocessing, and SageMaker AI Canvas (a no-code ML service) to generate baseline forecasts for monthly energy demand. However, the team now plans to build a custom machine learning (ML) model that can forecast future meter-usage patterns across all meter types. Which option satisfies the requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Build a single global forecasting model using the SageMaker AI DeepAR forecasting algorithm trained on all meter types to capture shared consumption patterns.
Train multiple forecasting models using the SageMaker AI Prophet algorithm, one for each meter type, to capture seasonal consumption patterns for individual devices.
options.rationale: because it introduces significant operational overhead. Managing 150 separate models increases complexity in training, deployment, and maintenance. Prophet is also better suited for simpler, univariate time series and doesn’t scale as efficiently as DeepAR for large, multi-series datasets.

options.text: Use SageMaker AI Autopilot to automatically create and tune a single predictive model for all meter types using the combined dataset.
options.rationale: because Autopilot is primarily optimized for tabular data and classification/regression tasks, not time series forecasting. It lacks native support for temporal dependencies and seasonality, which are critical for accurate meter usage predictions.

options.text: Create a single global forecasting model using the SageMaker AI XGBoost algorithm trained on all meter types to predict future consumption patterns.
options.rationale: because XGBoost is a powerful algorithm for tabular data, but not inherently designed for time series forecasting. You would typically need to manually engineer time-based features, which increases complexity and operational burden.

correct_text: Build a single global forecasting model using the SageMaker AI DeepAR forecasting algorithm trained on all meter types to capture shared consumption patterns.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A healthcare technology company is building an AI-powered patient support assistant on top of Amazon Bedrock. Company policy requires that the assistant never discuss specific medical diagnoses with patients. It must also block harmful or inappropriate content, mask personally identifiable information (PII) wherever it appears, and preserve audit trails to satisfy healthcare compliance reporting requirements. Both what patients type in and what the model generates in response must undergo content filtering based on the content’s sensitivity. To meet these needs, the company wants a Bedrock guardrails setup that enforces its policies reliably while keeping false positives to a minimum. The chosen approach must also support different handling strategies depending on the type and sensitivity of the content involved. Which of the following solutions will meet these requirements?

options.text: Build one guardrail and push every Content Filters category to its highest strength setting. Add medical diagnoses as a denied topic and supply example phrases that should trigger a block. Configure the Sensitive Information Filters so that every detected PII entity type is blocked outright. Attach this guardrail to every model inference request the assistant makes.
options.rationale: . Pushing every content filter category to its highest strength just increases the likelihood of false positives, working directly against the requirement to enforce policies with minimal false positives. Blocking every PII entity type outright also fails to provide multiple handling strategies for different types of sensitive content; the scenario specifically calls for differentiated treatment, such as masking less-critical PII while blocking higher-risk data, which a uniform block-everything approach does not offer.

options.text: Use Amazon Comprehend to detect PII entities in patient messages before they reach Bedrock, and use Amazon Macie to scan stored conversation logs for sensitive data. Apply a single Bedrock guardrail with Content Filters set to high for harmful content only.
options.rationale: . Amazon Comprehend can detect PII entities in text, but routing detection through Comprehend as a pre-processing step outside Bedrock Guardrails means the team must build and maintain custom integration logic instead of using Guardrails’ native, unified sensitive information filtering. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails help detect sensitive information, such as personally identifiable information (PII), in input prompts or model responses using sensitive information filters. This filter is a probabilistic machine learning (ML) based solution that is context-dependent and detects sensitive information based on the context within input prompts or model responses. Amazon Macie is designed to discover and classify sensitive data stored in Amazon S3, not to filter real-time conversational inputs and outputs, making it a mismatched tool for this use case. This approach also does not address the denied-topics requirement for medical diagnoses at all.

options.text: Set the Content Filters strength to medium for harmful content. Add medical diagnoses as a denied topic with a clear definition and sample phrases. Set the Sensitive Information Filters to mask PII in responses and block insurance details in inputs. Turn on input and output evaluation with custom blocked messages for audit logging.

Build three separate guardrails. One for harmful content, one for the medical diagnosis topic, and one for PII blocking through Sensitive Information Filters. Connect them in order using an AWS Step Functions workflow that routes each message based on its classification.
options.rationale: . Splitting protections across multiple guardrails chained together with AWS Step Functions introduces unnecessary complexity, orchestration overhead, and additional points of failure, when a single, well-configured guardrail can already combine content filters, denied topics, and sensitive information filters together. A guardrail must contain at least one filter and messaging for when prompts and user responses are blocked. You can opt to use the default messaging. You can add filters and iterate on your guardrail later. This fragmented design also does not clearly address minimizing false positives and adds custom conditional logic the team must build and maintain, rather than relying on Bedrock’s native evaluation of both input and output.

correct_text: Set the Content Filters strength to medium for harmful content. Add medical diagnoses as a denied topic with a clear definition and sample phrases. Set the Sensitive Information Filters to mask PII in responses and block insurance details in inputs. Turn on input and output evaluation with custom blocked messages for audit logging.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A data science team is leveraging Amazon SageMaker AI to build and deploy machine learning models for predictive analytics. The team also uses Amazon Comprehend to perform natural language processing (NLP) on text data as part of an analysis pipeline. The SageMaker notebook instances are deployed within an isolated Amazon VPC to ensure that the development work is secure. VPC interface endpoints were set up to establish private connectivity between the VPC and the SageMaker API. The team is also exploring the AWS Strands API as part of broader AI tooling initiatives. The team later discovers that unauthorized users from outside the VPC can still access the notebook instances through the internet, raising security concerns. How can the team limit access to the SageMaker notebook instances, ensuring only authorized VPC users can connect?

options.text: Update the security group for the notebook instances to restrict incoming traffic to only the CIDR blocks associated with the VPC. Apply this security group across all interfaces linked to the SageMaker notebook instances.
options.rationale: because configuring a security group only restricts traffic at the network interface level. While this approach controls access to the instances themselves, it does not prevent users from accessing the SageMaker API over the internet, which is required to interact with the notebook instances. Therefore, this method does not fully secure access to the notebook instances.

options.text: Configure an IAM policy that allows sagemaker:CreatePresignedNotebookInstanceUrl and sagemaker:DescribeNotebookInstance actions exclusively from VPC interface endpoints. Ensure this policy is applied to the appropriate IAM users, groups, and roles.
Set up VPC Traffic Mirroring to capture traffic to and from the notebook instances and identify unauthorized access attempts, enabling enhanced monitoring.
options.rationale: because VPC Traffic Mirroring is a monitoring tool that primarily captures and inspects network traffic. It does not block or restrict access to resources. While it helps in identifying unauthorized access attempts, it does not prevent them from occurring, making it unsuitable for securing the notebook instances themselves.

options.text: Apply VPC Endpoint Policies to control which IAM users or services can access SageMaker AI through the VPC interface endpoint, providing more granular access control for interactions with SageMaker AI.
options.rationale: because VPC Endpoint Policies typically control access to AWS services over the VPC endpoint but do not restrict access to the SageMaker notebook instances themselves. They manage which users or services can access the SageMaker API through the endpoint, but they do not secure the notebook instances from unauthorized access.

correct_text: Configure an IAM policy that allows sagemaker:CreatePresignedNotebookInstanceUrl and sagemaker:DescribeNotebookInstance actions exclusively from VPC interface endpoints. Ensure this policy is applied to the appropriate IAM users, groups, and roles.

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A Generative AI engineering team is developing a supervised image recognition model to accurately identify pandas from a diverse dataset of wildlife photographs. Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth is used to label 1,000 panda images and split the data into training and testing sets, reserving 100 images as a constant test set. Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels is then configured to train a custom image classification model capable of recognizing distinctive panda features such as fur patterns, posture, and environmental background. During the evaluation phase, the engineering team observes that the image classifier misclassifies several test images. A closer analysis reveals that in more than 75% of the misclassified images, the pandas appear upside down, indicating the model’s sensitivity to image orientation. The team must enhance the model’s ability to correctly identify pandas regardless of orientation, without collecting an entirely new dataset or extensively modifying the existing training pipeline. Which approach will most effectively enhance the model’s accuracy in addressing this specific misclassification issue?

options.text: Implement normalization preprocessing steps to make all images share a common scale and brightness distribution.
options.rationale: because normalization primarily standardizes image pixel intensity and brightness levels to ensure consistent numerical input during model training. While this process improves training stability and gradient performance, it does not enhance a model’s ability to recognize objects from different orientations or poses, which is the main issue described in the scenario.

options.text: Raise the number of training epochs to prolong optimization and reinforce feature representation within the existing dataset.
options.rationale: because increasing the number of epochs simply causes the model to iterate over the same dataset multiple times. This can reduce training loss but does not address the lack of visual diversity in the images. Without new data variations, the model remains sensitive to image orientation and may even overfit to existing patterns instead of learning rotational invariance.

options.text: Expand the existing training dataset by introducing data augmentation techniques such as image rotation, flipping, and scaling.
Apply transfer learning techniques to reuse a proven vision model’s base layers while retraining task-specific layers for panda identification.
options.rationale: because transfer learning typically accelerates model training and leverages existing learned features, but cannot overcome orientation-specific bias when the dataset lacks diversity. It improves feature extraction for similar visual patterns but does not replace the need for augmentation methods that expose the model to multiple orientations during training.

correct_text: Expand the existing training dataset by introducing data augmentation techniques such as image rotation, flipping, and scaling.

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: An organization is deploying a generative AI application that requires specific configuration flags to be updated dynamically without restarting the application. The infrastructure team needs to ensure that any configuration changes are validated against a schema before being deployed to the environment to prevent runtime errors. The application is running on an Amazon EC2 instance. Which solution should be implemented to manage these configurations efficiently?

options.text: Use AWS CloudFormation Guard to validate the configuration files and push updates via Amazon S3.
options.rationale: because CloudFormation Guard is primarily a policy-as-code tool used to validate CloudFormation templates and infrastructure-as-code (IaC) against compliance rules, not to manage dynamic application-level runtime configurations.

options.text: Implement AppConfig Agent on the EC2 instance to retrieve and cache configurations with pre-deployment validation.
Utilize Amazon DynamoDB Streams to trigger an AWS Lambda function that updates local configuration files.
options.rationale: because while Amazon DynamoDB Streams can track changes, it is an over-engineered solution for configuration management that does not provide the built-in validation, deployment strategies, or caching mechanisms offered by AppConfig.

options.text: Use Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to store application environment variables and configuration flags.
options.rationale: because Bedrock Prompt Management is simply designed for versioning and managing generative AI prompts, not for general application environment variables or infrastructure configuration flags.

correct_text: Implement AppConfig Agent on the EC2 instance to retrieve and cache configurations with pre-deployment validation.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A global e-commerce company is building a multilingual product description generator using Amazon Titan Text on Amazon Bedrock. The team plans to enhance the model’s domain understanding by fine-tuning it with proprietary product data in Amazon SageMaker AI before deploying it to production through Bedrock’s managed API. For compliance reasons, all model artifacts must be encrypted using AWS KMS, and API calls to the Bedrock endpoint must be logged and auditable. The company also wants to continuously monitor model latency and throughput across different regions to ensure consistent performance. Which solution provides a secure, compliant, and observable architecture for deploying and monitoring the Titan-based generative AI model?

options.text: Fine-tune the Titan model in SageMaker AI using training data stored in Amazon S3 with KMS encryption, deploy the model through Bedrock with a customer-managed KMS key, enable AWS CloudTrail for API auditing, and use Amazon CloudWatch metrics for Bedrock such as InvocationLatency to continuously monitor latency and throughput across regions.

Fine-tune the Titan model in SageMaker AI using data encrypted with SSE-S3, deploy it through an API Gateway endpoint in front of Bedrock, and use Amazon Macie to monitor for data exfiltration events.
options.rationale: because SSE-S3 lacks customer-managed key control and granular auditability that SSE-KMS provides, API Gateway is unnecessary in front of Bedrock’s managed endpoint, and Amazon Macie primarily focuses on discovering sensitive data in S3 rather than monitoring model invocations or performance.

options.text: Deploy the Titan model directly on Bedrock without fine-tuning, use AWS IAM roles to restrict access, and rely on AWS CloudTrail logs to monitor API calls. Monitor the model using the GenAI Observability feature in Amazon CloudWatch via the InvocationLatency, InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount metrics.
options.rationale: because it simply omits the required domain adaptation via fine-tuning and does not address encryption of training artifacts with customer-managed KMS keys, even though logging with CloudTrail is valid.

options.text: Train the Titan model entirely within SageMaker AI, export it to an Amazon EC2-based inference server with Amazon EBS encryption, and use AWS Config for compliance monitoring.
options.rationale: because moving inference to EC2 forfeits Bedrock’s managed security/scale and does not meet the requirement to deploy “through Bedrock’s managed API”; AWS Config tracks configuration state, not real-time model latency/throughput, which should be monitored via CloudWatch.

correct_text: Fine-tune the Titan model in SageMaker AI using training data stored in Amazon S3 with KMS encryption, deploy the model through Bedrock with a customer-managed KMS key, enable AWS CloudTrail for API auditing, and use Amazon CloudWatch metrics for Bedrock such as InvocationLatency to continuously monitor latency and throughput across regions.

category: AIP – Foundation Model Integration, Data Management, and Compliance
stem: A large-scale e-commerce platform is developing an AI-powered email filtering system that automatically identifies and flags malicious, spam, and phishing emails before reaching end users. The AI development team will implement this solution using Amazon SageMaker AI for model training and deployment, taking advantage of SageMaker’s managed environment for building and fine-tuning machine learning models. The system will rely on Amazon Comprehend to extract key entities and sentiment from incoming emails, helping the model identify potential threats. The training dataset consists of several thousand human-labeled emails, where each email is paired with a label of “spam” or “not spam”. The AI development team aims to improve the model’s performance by applying transfer learning using a Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model that was pretrained on a large corpus of text data. The goal is to fine-tune the pretrained BERT model on the labeled email dataset, which will allow the model to learn how to better classify email content. The pretrained BERT model weights need to be correctly loaded and used as the initialization point for fine-tuning, ensuring the model can effectively detect spam without requiring a full retraining process. Which approach will correctly initialize the BERT model to achieve this requirement?

options.text: Load the pretrained model weights for every layer and place an external classifier on top of the primary model output vector. Train the newly added classifier with the labeled dataset.
options.rationale: because this approach just stacks an additional layer on top of the original output without replacing the classifier, which prevents the model from adapting properly to the new task. The original output layer was trained for a different task, and leaving it unchanged introduces misalignment between the pretrained model’s representations and the specific requirements of the new classification task, reducing the effectiveness of fine-tuning.

options.text: Apply pretrained model parameters across all layers, then discard the existing final layer. Introduce a custom classifier and train it using the labeled data for spam detection.

Use the pretrained model weights for all transformer layers and attach a second classifier layer in parallel with the existing output layer. Train only this additional classifier using the labeled dataset.
options.rationale: because this method typically leads to conflicting decision-making processes within the model. By introducing a second classifier, the model tries to handle multiple outputs simultaneously, which can cause ambiguity and prevent the model from focusing on the correct target class, such as spam detection. This multi-output approach can complicate optimization and degrade overall model performance.

options.text: Initialize the model with pretrained weights, convert the output layer into a multi-task classifier that predicts multiple text classes beyond spam detection, and train this classifier using the labeled dataset.
options.rationale: because this is primarily designed for multi-task learning scenarios, not for a binary classification task like spam detection. Expanding the model to predict multiple classes introduces unnecessary complexity, making the model less efficient for the task at hand. By overcomplicating the model, the training process becomes more challenging and computationally expensive without providing any additional value for a specific binary task.

correct_text: Apply pretrained model parameters across all layers, then discard the existing final layer. Introduce a custom classifier and train it using the labeled data for spam detection.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A global clinical research organization (CRO) is designing a generative AI (GenAI) portal using Amazon Bedrock to analyze and extract insights from clinical trial protocols for various research teams. The portal must output structured records that contain a study design overview, a classification of patient safety risks, and operational bottlenecks flagged for investigator review. The generated output must adapt in vocabulary and style depending on the viewing audience, such as clinical investigators, biostatisticians, or regulatory compliance officers. Additionally, the portal must filter out toxic language, off-topic discussions, and protected health information (PHI). The organization wants to avoid hardcoding or decentralized management of prompt templates across different study teams. They also want to eliminate custom-written post-processing scripts to sanitize model outputs and require a mechanism to dynamically update safety and compliance filters without redeploying the core application. Which of the following solutions will meet these requirements with the LEAST maintenance overhead?

options.text: Set up Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to build reusable prompt templates along with variants tailored to each department. Enable Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with content category filters and sensitive information filters to prevent disallowed content from reaching users.

Leverage Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to establish baseline prompt templates. Achieve department-specific tone adjustments through system prompt variables. Set up Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to perform threshold tuning based on the target audience. Handle guardrail configuration changes through a custom-built internal administration API.
options.rationale: . It correctly uses Prompt Management and Guardrails, but adds a redundant custom-built internal administration API. Guardrails already exposes native APIs for creating and updating guardrails. Create a guardrail to detect and filter harmful content in your generative AI application. So a separate administration layer only adds unnecessary maintenance overhead. amazon

options.text: Use Bedrock Agents to orchestrate department-based instruction injection. Store response formatting rules in Amazon DynamoDB. Use AWS Step Functions to validate responses. Use Bedrock Guardrails only as a post-processing step after the GenAI concierge generates responses.
options.rationale: . Bedrock Agents is meant for orchestrating multi-step tasks and tool/API invocation, not simple prompt templating. Storing formatting rules in DynamoDB and validating with Step Functions requires custom schema design and state machine maintenance that Prompt Management already handles natively, and applying Guardrails only after generation means harmful content could already be produced before filtering.

options.text: Use Bedrock Knowledge Bases to store custom prompt templates. Create one AWS Lambda function to select department-specific prompts. Create a second Lambda function to call Amazon Comprehend to filter prohibited content from responses.
options.rationale: . Knowledge Bases is built for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), not for storing structured prompt templates. Maintaining two separate Lambda functions for prompt selection and Comprehend-based moderation also adds custom code and tuning effort that built-in Guardrails filtering already eliminates.

correct_text: Set up Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management to build reusable prompt templates along with variants tailored to each department. Enable Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with content category filters and sensitive information filters to prevent disallowed content from reaching users.

category: AIP – Operational Efficiency and Optimization for Generative AI Applications
stem: A company is deploying a fraud detection model using Amazon SageMaker AI and Amazon Comprehend in production. The model is designed to analyze transaction data, while Comprehend is used to extract key entities from transaction descriptions. The company wants to monitor the model’s performance over time, especially as fraud patterns evolve, and automatically re-train the model with the newly collected data to improve its accuracy. The company also needs to ensure that this process does not disrupt the production system. Which of the following should be implemented with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use SageMaker Ground Truth for labeling new data, then automate the retraining workflow using SageMaker Pipelines based on the labeled data.
options.rationale: because it introduces additional operational complexity. Ground Truth typically requires human or automated labeling, which adds latency and cost. While Pipelines help automate retraining, the need for labeled data increases overhead compared to using already captured inference data.

options.text: Implement SageMaker Debugger to track model performance and trigger retraining when the model crosses specific performance thresholds.
options.rationale: because Debugger is primarily designed for monitoring training jobs, not deployed endpoints. It doesn’t natively support inference-time monitoring or automatic retraining triggers based on production data, making it unsuitable for this use case.

options.text: Use SageMaker Experiments to track model training runs and collect new data. Trigger model retraining based on experiment results.
options.rationale: because SageMaker Experiments is meant for tracking and comparing training runs, not for monitoring deployed models or collecting inference data. It lacks built-in mechanisms to detect drift or trigger retraining based on real-time production performance.

options.text: Enable SageMaker Model Monitor with Data Capture on the deployed endpoint to collect input/output data, and use this data for automated model retraining.

correct_text: Enable SageMaker Model Monitor with Data Capture on the deployed endpoint to collect input/output data, and use this data for automated model retraining.

category: AIP – Implementation and Integration
stem: A global publishing company manages a large repository of multimedia content, including PDFs, images, audio files, and video recordings from news articles, interviews, and webinars. The company seeks to automate the extraction of insights such as key topics and relevant entities to help journalists and editors quickly access information. The company aims to build a generative AI-powered research assistant capable of answering natural language queries like, “Which article mentioned climate adaptation in Southeast Asia and included aerial images?” The company plans to use Amazon Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) for processing unstructured media and extracting structured insights, and Amazon SageMaker AI to host the generative AI model for context‑aware response generation. Which approach will best meet the requirements?

options.text: Use Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) to process the media files, store the raw content in Amazon S3, and deploy a custom AWS Lambda function to create your own vector database outside of Bedrock Knowledge Bases before passing it to SageMaker AI.
options.rationale: because Storing raw content in Amazon S3 and creating a custom vector database outside of Bedrock Knowledge Bases simply adds unnecessary complexity and manual steps. Bedrock Knowledge Bases is specifically designed to store and index structured insights for semantic search, streamlining the retrieval process. Creating a custom vector database with Lambda bypasses the optimized capabilities of Bedrock Knowledge Bases, making the solution less efficient and more difficult to manage.

options.text: Leverage Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) to process documents, images, audio, and video, index the results in Bedrock Knowledge Bases for semantic search, and then input the retrieved context into a foundation model via SageMaker AI for response generation.

Utilize Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) to process media files, analyze the structured content using Amazon Comprehend for entity and sentiment extraction, and then forward the results to a foundation model hosted on Amazon EC2 for generating answers.
options.rationale: because hosting the foundation model on EC2 instead of SageMaker AI adds unnecessary operational overhead. SageMaker AI is the recommended service for deploying machine learning models as it provides a fully managed environment that simplifies model deployment, scaling, and integration with other AWS services. Using EC2 would require more manual setup and management, which is inefficient compared to the streamlined capabilities of SageMaker AI.

options.text: Employ Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) to process all media types and directly supply the structured output into a foundation model via SageMaker AI, bypassing the use of a knowledge base.
options.rationale: because bypassing Bedrock Knowledge Bases only eliminates the important step of indexing and semantic search. Bedrock Knowledge Bases are important for retrieving contextually relevant content based on user queries. Without using a knowledge base, the solution misses the advantage of optimized context retrieval, which could lead to less accurate or slower responses from the generative model. The knowledge base is key to ensuring fast and accurate retrieval of relevant content.

correct_text: Leverage Bedrock Data Automation (BDA) to process documents, images, audio, and video, index the results in Bedrock Knowledge Bases for semantic search, and then input the retrieved context into a foundation model via SageMaker AI for response generation.

category: AIP – Testing, Validation, and Troubleshooting
stem: A global e-commerce company is developing a product return prediction model using the Amazon SageMaker XGBoost algorithm to identify which orders are most likely to result in customer returns. Transactional and behavioral data are stored in Amazon Redshift, and the data engineering team utilizes SageMaker Data Wrangler to clean and prepare training features, including product category, customer sentiment, and delivery delays. After deploying the model, the team observes that while the training Area Under the Curve (AUC) is exceptionally high, the validation performance drops significantly. Model explainability reports from SageMaker Clarify reveal that the model is overly sensitive to a few dominant features like product price and region, suggesting overfitting to patterns in the training set. The team decides to tune the model’s hyperparameters to reduce model complexity and improve its ability to generalize to new data. Which hyperparameter modification would best help reduce overfitting and improve validation performance for this XGBoost model?

options.text: Increase the max_depth hyperparameter to allow deeper trees that can better capture relationships between rare features.
options.rationale: . Increasing max_depth would typically make each tree more complex and more prone to overfitting. While deeper trees can capture rare feature interactions, they also simply memorize noise and outliers from the training data rather than learning general patterns. In this scenario, where the model already performs exceptionally well on training data but poorly on validation data, increasing max_depth would only worsen overfitting instead of reducing it.

options.text: Decrease the min_child_weight parameter to allow each leaf node to split more easily, capturing additional complexity in the dataset.
options.rationale: . Reducing min_child_weight lowers the minimum number of observations required to create a new leaf node, which typically increases the model’s complexity. Doing so encourages the model to just create more splits, even for insignificant variations in data, leading to deeper trees and more overfitting. Since the goal is to simplify the model and prevent overfitting, decreasing min_child_weight moves in the opposite direction of what’s needed.

options.text: Increase the colsample_bytree parameter to ensure each tree uses a greater subset of features and improves model variance.
options.rationale: . Increasing colsample_bytree allows the model to use a larger fraction of available features for each tree, which primarily increases feature diversity rather than reducing overfitting. Although this can sometimes help stabilize training, it does not directly limit model complexity. In fact, allowing more features per tree can simply make the model more likely to overfit on correlated inputs if dominant features consistently drive splits.

options.text: Decrease the value of the max_depth hyperparameter to limit tree complexity and prevent overfitting on dominant patterns in the training data.

correct_text: Decrease the value of the max_depth hyperparameter to limit tree complexity and prevent overfitting on dominant patterns in the training data.

category: AIP – AI Safety, Security, and Governance
stem: A financial services company uses Amazon SageMaker Studio notebooks for data exploration and SageMaker Autopilot to train ML models on customer data stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The dataset contains sensitive financial information, and compliance policies require that all data traffic remain within the AWS private network. During an audit, the security team discovers that SageMaker Studio is accessing S3 over the public internet. The AI developer must reconfigure the environment to ensure that all data transfers between SageMaker and S3 occur securely within AWS’s internal network while maintaining full functionality for Studio notebooks and Autopilot jobs. Which configuration should the developer implement to meet this requirement?
